stemBlocks.value: Think first: Both the top and the bottom will factorise, and the whole point is to reveal a factor they share.

solutionSteps.instruction: Factorise the numerator by removing the common factor x.
Factorise the denominator as a difference of two squares.
Write the fraction in factorised form.

strategyBlocks.value: Factorise the numerator by taking out x, factorise the denominator as a difference of two squares, then cancel the common bracket.

whyThisWorks.value: An algebraic fraction only simplifies when the top and bottom share a whole factor, not merely a matching term. Factorising turns a sum into a product, and only then is (x + 7) a genuine factor of both parts that can be divided out. The difference of two squares is the key here because x² − 49 hides the very bracket the numerator produces.

commonErrors.misconception: Cancelling the x² terms or the individual numbers straight from x² + 7x over x² − 49 without factorising first.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Cancelling the x² terms or the individual numbers straight from x² + 7x over x² − 49 without factorising first.
Avoid this: Writing x² − 49 as (x − 7)² instead of (x + 7)(x − 7).

commonErrors.misconception: Forgetting to state or notice that x cannot equal 7 or −7.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Forgetting to state or notice that x cannot equal 7 or −7.

examTip.value: Whenever you see a subtraction of two perfect squares, test it as a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b) before trying anything else — it is the fastest factorisation in the syllabus.
